title: What Are r/truefilm's thoughts on Sling Blade and Thornton's performance?

commenti.body:
I always thought it was terrible. the redneck step dad I thought was great. I had to look up my favorite line from the movie. what's the deal with I am Sam?

>Hey is this the kind of retard that drools and rubs sh*t in his hair and all that, 'cause I'm gonna have a hard time eatin' 'round that kind of thing now. Just like I am with antique furniture and midgets. You know that, I can't so much as drink a damn glass of water around a midget or a piece of antique furniture.
Penn received a lot of critique from I am Sam, as well as good reviews too. it was polarizing

Personally, when it comes to portrayals of disabled people, there are very few that pass the test. Sling Blade (and Billy Bob Thornton) and My Left Foot (and Daniel Day-Lewis) are two that always stick out for me.

I'm not from the south, but I have plenty of family from the south, and I've visited countless times. Everything about Sling Blade feels real to me. Billy Bob is from the south, and I've seen him talk about how angry it makes him to see southern characters be portrayed disingenuously and/or with ridiculous accents. I think John Ritter is the only actor in the film who isn't from a southern background, and the fact that he plays an "outsider" type of character makes total sense. Billy Bob is unrecognizable, and even a superstar musician like Dwight Yoakum blends in without much effort. The kid is fantastic, the mom is just as good, the bit-part supporting cast couldn't have been better, and the cameo by Robert Duvall was perfect.

The story is powerful, and I'm always left moved when the movie ends. As an indie film, it's even more impressive. From my perspective, it ages better than it faired in its own time. It managed to make such an impact in the culture that people parodied it, and mimicked Billy Bob's facial expressions. I remember hearing the grunts and "French-fried taters" everywhere for a time. That's when it was still common for people to talk about mentally disabled people like Dwight Yoakum's character did - in public, without anyone batting an eye at it. But nobody ever said the movie or acting was silly or anything. It was actually the opposite. Strange how that goes. Reminds me of Brando in The Godfather or something. It's so good that it takes on a life of its own, and becomes iconic.

I actually have never heard anyone in the real world say anything bad about the film.

I love it! It's no secret that Thornton is a fan of Cormac McCarthy. Thornton's next project was an adaptation of McCarthy's 'All the Pretty Horses,' but it was basically maimed in the editing room by a displeased Harvey Weinstein following a disagreement with Thornton over the production of 'Sling Blade.' 

For me, 'Sling Blade' is a brilliant Southern Gothic, reminiscent of McCarthy's style, portraying a novelistic, "human condition" depiction of working-class (and below) white rural types. (I'm not from the States, so disagreement with this point is welcome.) Particularly SG is Carl's story of how he ended up in the hospital, as well as his backstory with his younger sibling. 

I've actually seen the director's cut, and to be honest, it did feel like a poor Southern version of 'Forrest Gump.' As it happens, Weinstein was right to make the cuts he did, despite the fallout that led to the mangling of 'All the Pretty Horses.' I think where 'I Am Sam' potentially fails (for me) is in its Hollywood nature. It feels more like Oscar bait, which 'Sling Blade' fortunately avoids by having a lower budget and an early '90s Miramax arthouse vibe. Incredible soundtrack by Daniel Lanois too!

Billy Bob Thornton's performance in "Sling Blade" has experienced a shift in perception over time. Initially acclaimed and earning him an Oscar for Best Adapted Screenplay and a Best Actor nomination, his portrayal of Karl Childers was praised for its depth and authenticity​ ([Roger Ebert](https://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/sling-blade-1996))​. However, some modern viewers now see his performance as bordering on parody, similar to how Sean Penn's "I Am Sam" was later critiqued​​.

Despite this, "Sling Blade" remains highly regarded for its storytelling, character development, and strong supporting performances by actors like Dwight Yoakam and John Ritter. The film's craftsmanship continues to be appreciated, making it a significant work from the 1990s​.
